## Introduction

Shootings occur in every major municipality in the world, which makes the City
of New York no exception. Across the five boroughs and their numerous precincts,
NYPD officers react to and produce meticulous notes on each case. This brief
report will, therefore, present the main findings from the historical NYPD
Shooting Incident Data set, with the newest version published by the City of
New York on NYC OpenData [1], which includes every shooting incident recorded by
the NYPD since 2006. The text answers three research questions: (1) what are the
long-term trends of shooting incidents for the City as a whole and for each
borough (with observations aggregated to monthly frequency to employ time-series
models), (2) are shootings distributed uniformly across boroughs and precincts,
and (3) which geographical or victim characteristics contribute to a fatal
outcome (i.e., the incident being declared a murder). Each research question is
complemented with a formal statistical hypothesis (or a statistical model)
tested at the standard 5% significance level ($\alpha=0.05$):

- **H1**. Monthly reported incidents have a statistically significant linear
  trend, i.e., $\beta_1 \neq 0$ in $y_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 t$.

- **H2**. Within each borough, incidents are distributed uniformly under a
  Pearson's $\chi^2$ goodness-of-fit test.

- **H3**. The possibility of an incident being classified as a murder depends on
  precinct, victim age group, sex, and/or race, based on a logistic
  regression model $\log(\frac{p_i}{1-p_i}) = \beta_0 + \sum_i \beta_i x_i$, in
  which $\exists_{\beta_i}\ \beta_i \neq 0$.

To compile this report, R packages `tidyverse` and `lubridate` were employed for
data processing, alongside `ggplot2` for visualization and the `chisq.test()`,
`lm()` and `glm()` functions for statistical modeling. All R code is embedded
into the R Markdown document to ensure its reproducibility. The original CSV
dataset, downloaded from Coursera, is accessed at
`./DATA/NYPD_Shooting_Incident_Data__Historic_.csv`. The report is subdivided
into five parts: data description and processing, time trend analysis, spatial
structure analysis, (logistic) incident classification model, and discussion of
potential data- and method-related bias.

## Data Description and Processing

```{r hidden1, include = FALSE}
RAW         <- read_csv('./DATA/NYPD_Shooting_Incident_Data__Historic_.csv')
n_rows      <- nrow(RAW)
n_cols      <- ncol(RAW)
n_na        <- sum(is.na(RAW))
n_incidents <- n_distinct(RAW$INCIDENT_KEY,      na.rm = TRUE)
date        <- as.Date(RAW$OCCUR_DATE,          format =  "%m/%d/%Y")
datetime    <- lubridate::mdy_hms(
               paste(RAW$OCCUR_DATE, RAW$OCCUR_TIME),
               tz = "America/New_York"
)
t_min       <- format(min(datetime,              na.rm = TRUE),
                                                "%B %d, %Y at %H:%M")
t_max       <- format(max(datetime,              na.rm = TRUE),
                                                "%B %d, %Y at %H:%M")
boroughs    <- names(sort(table(RAW$BORO),  decreasing = TRUE))
murders     <- mean(RAW$STATISTICAL_MURDER_FLAG, na.rm = TRUE)
vic_male    <- mean(RAW$VIC_SEX == "M",          na.rm = TRUE)
```

The raw (unprocessed) NYPD Shooting Incident dataset consists of
`r number_fmt(n_rows)` rows and `r n_cols` columns, corresponding to
`r number_fmt(n_incidents)` unique incidents (one row per victim) recorded
between `r t_min` and `r t_max`. The data cover `r length(boroughs)` boroughs
(`r paste(boroughs, collapse = ", ")`). Only about `r round(murders * 100, 1)`%
of the records were classified as murders with predominantly
`r if (vic_male > 0.5) "male" else "female or other"` victims
(`r round(100 * max(vic_male, 1 - vic_male), 1)`%). Given that the data
comprises `r number_fmt(n_na)` missing values, excessively detailed temporal
information (dates and times) for the intended monthly time-series analysis,
additional columns, which will not be used in the analysis, column types
requiring conversion (e.g., character instead of factor), abbreviated variable
names (e.g., BORO instead of BOROUGH), and minor value inconsistencies (e.g.,
"1022" must be recoded `NA` for the VIC_AGE_GROUP), the raw dataset required
several preprocessing steps: employing `tidyverse`'s `select()`, `mutate()`,
`rename()`, `group_by()`, and `summarize()` functions to obtain a modified
tibble `NYPD`.

```{r tidy, echo = TRUE, results = 'hide', message = FALSE}
NYPD <- read_csv('./DATA/NYPD_Shooting_Incident_Data__Historic_.csv')        %>%
        select(c(OCCUR_DATE, BORO, PRECINCT, STATISTICAL_MURDER_FLAG,
                 VIC_AGE_GROUP, VIC_SEX, VIC_RACE))                          %>%
        mutate(  VIC_AGE_GROUP = na_if(VIC_AGE_GROUP, "1022"),
                 across(where(is.character), ~na_if(.x, "UNKNOWN")),
                 across(where(is.character), ~na_if(.x, "(null)")),
                 OCCUR_DATE              = mdy(OCCUR_DATE), BORO = factor(BORO),
                 MONTH                   = floor_date(OCCUR_DATE, "month"),
                 BORO                    = factor(str_to_title(BORO)),
                 PRECINCT                = factor(PRECINCT),
                 STATISTICAL_MURDER_FLAG = factor(STATISTICAL_MURDER_FLAG),
                 VIC_AGE_GROUP           = factor(VIC_AGE_GROUP),
                 VIC_SEX                 = factor(VIC_SEX),
                 VIC_RACE                = factor(str_to_title(VIC_RACE)),
                 SHOOTINGS               = 1)                                %>%
        group_by(MONTH, BORO, PRECINCT, STATISTICAL_MURDER_FLAG,
                                        VIC_AGE_GROUP, VIC_SEX, VIC_RACE)    %>%
                 summarize(SHOOTINGS     = sum(SHOOTINGS,  na.rm = TRUE))    %>%
        ungroup()                                                            %>%
        rename(  BOROUGH                 = BORO)                             %>%
        rename(  MURDER                  = STATISTICAL_MURDER_FLAG)          %>%
        rename(  VICTIM_AGE_GROUP        = VIC_AGE_GROUP)                    %>%
        rename(  VICTIM_SEX              = VIC_SEX)                          %>%
        rename(  VICTIM_RACE             = VIC_RACE)
```

```{r hidden2, include = FALSE}
n_rows        <- nrow(NYPD)
n_cols        <- ncol(NYPD)
n_na_tidy     <- sum( is.na(NYPD))
m_min         <- format(min(NYPD$MONTH, na.rm = TRUE), "%B %Y")
m_max         <- format(max(NYPD$MONTH, na.rm = TRUE), "%B %Y")
murders       <- NYPD                                                        %>%
                 filter(!is.na(MURDER))                                      %>%
                 summarize(
                      PERCENT = sum(SHOOTINGS[MURDER == "TRUE"])               / 
                                sum(SHOOTINGS)
                 )                                                           %>%
                 pull(PERCENT)
max_age_group <- NYPD                                                        %>%
                 filter(NYPD$MURDER == "TRUE")                               %>%
                 group_by(VICTIM_AGE_GROUP)                                  %>%
                       summarize(SHOOTINGS = sum(SHOOTINGS, na.rm = TRUE))   %>%
                 ungroup()                                                   %>%
                 arrange(desc(   SHOOTINGS))                                 %>%
                 slice_max(      SHOOTINGS,  n = 1,     with_ties = FALSE)   %>%
                 pull(    VICTIM_AGE_GROUP)

max_sex       <- NYPD                                                        %>%
                 filter(NYPD$MURDER == "TRUE")                               %>%
                 group_by(VICTIM_SEX)                                        %>%
                       summarize(SHOOTINGS = sum(SHOOTINGS, na.rm = TRUE))   %>%
                 ungroup()                                                   %>%
                 arrange(desc(   SHOOTINGS))                                 %>%
                 slice_max(      SHOOTINGS,  n = 1,     with_ties = FALSE)   %>%
                 pull(VICTIM_SEX)

max_race      <- NYPD                                                        %>%
                 filter(NYPD$MURDER == "TRUE")                               %>%
                 group_by(VICTIM_RACE)                                       %>%
                       summarize(SHOOTINGS = sum(SHOOTINGS, na.rm = TRUE))   %>%
                 ungroup()                                                   %>%
                 arrange(desc(SHOOTINGS))                                    %>%
                 slice_max(SHOOTINGS,  n=1,      with_ties = FALSE)          %>%
                 pull(VICTIM_RACE)
```

The obtained tibble consists of `r number_fmt(n_rows)` rows and `r n_cols`
columns, where `MONTH` and `SHOOTINGS` were additionally created, with
`r number_fmt(n_na_tidy)` missing values (i.e., a
`r round(100 * (1 - n_na_tidy / n_na), 1)`% reduction in the number of missing
cells), corrected value labels, and readable variable names. To summarize the
tibble `NYPD`, between `r m_min` and `r m_max`,
**`r number_fmt(sum(NYPD$SHOOTINGS))` cases** were reported, out of
which `r number_fmt(sum((NYPD %>% filter(BOROUGH=="Brooklyn"     ))$SHOOTINGS))`
in Brooklyn,
      `r number_fmt(sum((NYPD %>% filter(BOROUGH=="Bronx"        ))$SHOOTINGS))`
in the Bronx,
      `r number_fmt(sum((NYPD %>% filter(BOROUGH=="Manhattan"    ))$SHOOTINGS))`
in Manhattan,
      `r number_fmt(sum((NYPD %>% filter(BOROUGH=="Queens"       ))$SHOOTINGS))`
in Queens, and
      `r number_fmt(sum((NYPD %>% filter(BOROUGH=="Staten Island"))$SHOOTINGS))`
in Staten Island.
**`r number_fmt(sum(NYPD$SHOOTINGS[NYPD$MURDER=="TRUE"], na.rm = TRUE))`** were
identified as murders (**`r round(murders * 100, 1)`%**), with the most victims
in the **`r max_age_group`**
**age group**, **`r if (max_sex == "M") "male" else "female or other"`**, and
**`r if (max_race == "Black") "African Americans" else str_to_lower(max_race)`**
in terms of race. The `summary()` output is below.

```{r summary, echo = TRUE}
summary(NYPD)
```

## Analysis of Time Trends

Aggregated monthly data show an uneven distribution of shooting incidents over
time and across boroughs with a declining linear trend, where the steepest
decline was observed in Brooklyn (see Table 1). Considering the spatial
distribution of New York City's population, the Bronx (No. 4 by population)
accounted for the second largest number of reported incidents (i.e., a higher
rate per 1000 inhabitants), while Manhattan and Queens (No. 2 and 3) registered
substantially fewer cases. Figure 1 also reveals periods of high and low shooting
activity, including a citywide spike during the COVID-19 pandemic. This
substantial increase may have been associated with socio-economic factors, such
as social isolation during the government-imposed lockdowns, declining incomes,
job losses, etc. -- i.e., potential relationships that require further
investigation.

```{r figure1, echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, fig.height = 3.8, fig.pos = "H"}
ggplot(NYPD                                                                  %>%
       group_by( MONTH, BOROUGH)                                             %>%
                summarize(SHOOTINGS  = sum(SHOOTINGS, na.rm = TRUE))         %>%
       ungroup()                                                             %>%
       bind_rows(NYPD                                                        %>%
                 group_by(MONTH)                                             %>%
                summarize(SHOOTINGS  = sum(SHOOTINGS, na.rm = TRUE),
                .groups          = "drop")                                  %>%
                 mutate(BOROUGH  = "Total")
       ),       aes(x = MONTH, y = SHOOTINGS, group     = BOROUGH))            +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, linewidth = 0.5, color = "red")  +
  facet_wrap(~BOROUGH, axes = "all_x", axis.labels = "all_x")                  +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma)                                   +
  labs(
    title = paste0("Figure 1. Reported shooting incidents, ",
                   as.character(m_min), "-", as.character(m_max)),
    x = "Month",
    y = "Reported shooting incidents"
  )                                                                            +
  theme_minimal()
```

The formal statistical test of **H1** is tied to coefficients $\beta_1$ from six
linear regression models `lm(SHOOTINGS ~ MONTH SEQUENCE)`, i.e., for each
borough and the dataset as a whole, with the `MONTH` encoded with the help of
`seq_along()` into a time-series sequence. Table 1 comprises the slopes, their
standard errors, the two-sided p-values, and the $R^2$ (coefficient of
determination) of the fit. Apart from Manhattan, the remaining coefficients
are non-zero at the 5% significance level ($\alpha=0.05$), although the models
reveal weak explanatory power -- i.e., potential additional factors influencing
the number of shooting incidents, such as a unit root.

```{r table1, echo = TRUE}
NYPD                                                                         %>%
group_by( MONTH, BOROUGH)                                                    %>%
         summarize(SHOOTINGS = sum(SHOOTINGS), .groups = "drop")             %>%
bind_rows(NYPD                                                               %>%
          group_by(MONTH) %>%
         summarize(SHOOTINGS = sum(SHOOTINGS), .groups = "drop")             %>%
          mutate(BOROUGH                               = "Total")
)                                                                            %>%
  filter(!is.na(BOROUGH),   !is.na(MONTH))                                   %>%
 arrange(BOROUGH, MONTH) %>%
group_by(BOROUGH) %>%
         summarize(MODEL = list(summary(lm(SHOOTINGS ~ seq_along(MONTH)))))  %>%
transmute(
         Borough = BOROUGH,
         Slope   = sapply(MODEL, \(m) m$coefficients[2, 1]),
         SE      = sapply(MODEL, \(m) m$coefficients[2, 2]),
         P       = sapply(MODEL, \(m) m$coefficients[2, 4]),
         R2      = sapply(MODEL, \(m) m$r.squared)
)                                                                            %>%
knitr::kable(digits  = 3,
             caption = "Linear trends in reported shooting incidents")
```

## Analysis of Spatial Structure

``` {r hidden3, include = FALSE}
precincts     <- NYPD                                                        %>%
                 group_by(BOROUGH, PRECINCT)                                 %>%
                       summarize(SHOOTINGS = sum(SHOOTINGS, na.rm = TRUE),
                                 .groups   = "drop")                         %>%
                 group_by(BOROUGH)                                           %>%
                       slice_max(order_by  = SHOOTINGS,         n = 10,
                                 with_ties = FALSE)                          %>%
                 ungroup()
```

Figure 2 demonstrates the distribution of shooting incidents by precinct.
Namely, the three precincts with the most reported incidents are **No.**
**`r (precincts                                                              %>%
slice_max(order_by = SHOOTINGS, n = 3, with_ties = FALSE))$PRECINCT          %>%
paste(collapse = ", ")`** citywide,    **No.**
**`r (precincts %>% filter(BOROUGH == "Bronx")                               %>%
slice_max(order_by = SHOOTINGS, n = 3, with_ties = FALSE))$PRECINCT          %>%
paste(collapse = ", ")`** in the Bronx, (the above-mentioned)    **No.**
**`r (precincts %>% filter(BOROUGH == "Brooklyn")                            %>%
slice_max(order_by = SHOOTINGS, n = 3, with_ties = FALSE))$PRECINCT          %>%
paste(collapse = ", ")`** in Brooklyn, **No.**
**`r (precincts %>% filter(BOROUGH == "Manhattan")                           %>%
slice_max(order_by = SHOOTINGS, n = 3, with_ties = FALSE))$PRECINCT          %>%
paste(collapse = ", ")`** in Manhattan, **No.**
**`r (precincts %>% filter(BOROUGH == "Queens")                              %>%
slice_max(order_by = SHOOTINGS, n = 3, with_ties = FALSE))$PRECINCT          %>%
paste(collapse = ", ")`** in Queens, and **No.**
**`r (precincts %>% filter(BOROUGH == "Staten Island")                       %>%
slice_max(order_by = SHOOTINGS, n = 3, with_ties = FALSE))$PRECINCT          %>%
paste(collapse = ", ")`** in Staten Island. These findings strongly indicate a
non-uniform distribution of the examined data.

```{r figure2, echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, fig.height = 3.8, fig.pos = "H"}
ggplot(NYPD                                                                  %>%
       group_by( BOROUGH, PRECINCT)                                          %>%
                summarize(SHOOTINGS  = sum(SHOOTINGS,       na.rm = TRUE))   %>%
       ungroup()                                                             %>%
       bind_rows(NYPD                                                        %>%
                 group_by(PRECINCT)                                          %>%
                summarize(SHOOTINGS  = sum(SHOOTINGS,       na.rm = TRUE),
                .groups         = "drop")                                    %>%
                 mutate(BOROUGH = "Total")
       )                                                                     %>%
       group_by( BOROUGH)                                                    %>%
                slice_max(order_by = SHOOTINGS, n = 10, with_ties = FALSE)   %>%
       ungroup(),    aes(x = reorder(PRECINCT, SHOOTINGS), y = SHOOTINGS))     +
  geom_col(width = 0.7)                                                        +
  coord_flip()                                                                 +
  facet_wrap(~ BOROUGH, scales  = "free_y", axes        = "all_x",
                                            axis.labels = "all_x")             +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(
    title = paste0("Figure 2. Top ten precincts by incidents, ",
                   as.character(m_min), "-", as.character(m_max)),
    x = "Precinct",
    y = "Reported shooting incidents"
  )                                                                            +
  theme_minimal()
```

The formal statistical test of **H2** is based on Pearson's chi-square
goodness-of-fit test `chisq.test(SHOOTINGS)` applied to six distributions of
reported shooting incidents across precincts, i.e., for each borough and the
dataset as a whole, with the null hypothesis assuming a uniform distribution of
incidents ($H_0: p_1 = p_2 = \cdots = p_k = 1/k$), where $k$ is the number of
precincts, and a p-value precision of $0.001$. The resulting Table 2 comprises
the $\chi^2$ statistics, degrees of freedom, and upper-tail p-values. $H_0$ is
rejected in all cases at the 5% significance level ($\alpha=0.05$), confirming a
statistically significant non-uniform distribution of shooting incidents across
precincts, which may reflect variations in population density, socio-economic
conditions, etc. -- i.e., potential relationships meriting further investigation
with the help of statistical (quantitative) modeling.

```{r table2, echo = TRUE}
NYPD                                                                         %>%
group_by( BOROUGH, PRECINCT)                                                 %>%
         summarize(SHOOTINGS = sum(SHOOTINGS), .groups = "drop")             %>%
bind_rows(NYPD                                                               %>%
          group_by(PRECINCT)                                                 %>%
         summarize(SHOOTINGS = sum(SHOOTINGS), .groups = "drop")             %>%
          mutate(BOROUGH                               = "Total")
)                                                                            %>%
  filter(!is.na(BOROUGH),   !is.na(PRECINCT))                                %>%
group_by( BOROUGH)                                                           %>%
         summarize(TEST = list(chisq.test(SHOOTINGS)))                       %>%
transmute(
         Borough = BOROUGH,
         Chi2    = sapply(TEST, \(m) unname(m$statistic)),
         DF      = sapply(TEST, \(m) unname(m$parameter)),
         P       = sapply(TEST, \(m) m$p.value)
)                                                                            %>%
mutate(P = scales::pvalue(P, accuracy = 0.001))                              %>%
knitr::kable(digits  = 3,
             caption = "Pearson chi-square tests of uniform distribution")
```

## Incident Classification Model

In order to identify the probability and corresponding odds of a shooting
incident being classified as a murder, -- which may provide valuable insights
for police precincts in allocating resources between calls, anticipating risks,
or developing potential preventive measures -- the following logistic regression
(a generalized linear model of the binomial family with a logit link) is
employed, with the log-odds modeled as a function of `PRECINCT` (`P`),
`VICTIM_AGE_GROUP` (`A`), `VICTIM_SEX` (`S`), and `VICTIM_RACE` (`R`). Its
predictors (features) were selected to reflect geography -- given the
above-established non-uniformity of distribution of shooting incidents across
precincts -- and demographics, specifically victim characteristics, given
the limited availability of information (a higher proportion of missing values)
on other potentially relevant predictors in the original (raw) dataset.

$$
\log\left(\frac{P(\text{MURDER}=1)}{1-P(\text{MURDER}=1)}\right)
= \beta_0
+ \sum_{j=1}^{J_P}\beta_{P_j}P_j
+ \sum_{j=1}^{J_A}\beta_{A_j}A_j
+ \sum_{j=1}^{J_S}\beta_{S_j}S_j
+ \sum_{j=1}^{J_R}\beta_{R_j}R_j
$$

The results of the `glm()` function estimated on the tibble `NYPD`, aggregated
across `BOROUGH` and `MONTH` with `SHOOTINGS` set as frequency weights, are
presented in Tables 3 and 4, and the corresponding R code below.

```{r model, echo = TRUE, results = 'hide'}
model <- glm(
  MURDER ~        PRECINCT + VICTIM_AGE_GROUP + VICTIM_SEX + VICTIM_RACE,
  data = NYPD                                                                %>%
         group_by(PRECINCT,  MURDER,
                             VICTIM_AGE_GROUP,  VICTIM_SEX,  VICTIM_RACE)    %>%
                  summarise(SHOOTINGS = sum(SHOOTINGS), .groups = "drop"),
  weights = SHOOTINGS,
  family = binomial()
)
```

Following the model, the formal statistical test of **H3** is
$H_0: \forall_{\beta_{x_j}}\ \beta_{x_j} = 0$ against
$H_1: \exists_{\beta_{x_j}}\ \beta_{x_j} \neq 0$, where
$x_j \in \{P_j, A_j, S_j, R_j\}$. Table 3 comprises the statistically
significant coefficients $\beta_{x_j}$ (log-odds) and equivalent odds ratios
$exp(\beta_{x_j})$  at the 5% significance level ($\alpha=0.05$) (i.e., the
table is truncated given the number of precincts in the dataset), their
standard errors, and the two-sided p-values. Individual $\beta_{x_j}$ indicate
significant odds differences across police precincts and victim age groups. On
the one hand, relative to Precinct 1 (the reference category), 28 precincts
have significantly lower odds of a murder incident, with odds ratios ranging
from 0.164 (Precinct 7) to 0.448 (Precinct 73) and standard errors being
near-identical ($\approx 0.40-0.60$). On the other hand, victim age group
shows a clear increasing pattern: relative to victims under 18 (the reference
category), the odds of a murder incident are ca. 29%, 81%, 111%, and
169% higher for ages 18–24, 25–44, 45–64, and 65+ respectively, with
significantly lower standard errors ($\approx 0.06-0.15$). No level of victim
sex or race, included in the logistic regression equation, was found to be
statistically significant at the 5% level.

```{r table3, echo = TRUE}
as.data.frame(summary(model)$coefficients)                                   %>%
tibble::rownames_to_column("Predictor")                                      %>%
filter(`Pr(>|z|)` < 0.05)                                                    %>%
transmute(
  Predictor,
  `Coefficient (log-odds)` = Estimate,
  `Odds ratio`             = exp(Estimate),
  `Std. error`             = `Std. Error`,
  `P`                      = scales::pvalue(`Pr(>|z|)`, accuracy = 0.001)
)                                                                            %>%
knitr::kable(
  digits  = 3,
  caption = "Statistically significant logistic regression coefficients"
)
```

Furthermore, the deviance-based likelihood-ratio (LR) test rejects the null
hypothesis of joint insignificance of the included predictors
$\chi^2(87) = 435.603$, with a p-value smaller than $0.001$, providing further
statistical support for `H_1` (see Table 4). Still, McFadden's
pseudo-$R^2$ of 0.015 indicates only a ca. 1.5% improvement in log-likelihood
relative to the intercept-only model, suggesting limited explanatory power and
reducing the practical significance of the findings. Thus, additional features
should be considered in further investigation.

```{r table4, echo = TRUE}
tibble(
  Statistic = c(
    "Observations", "Null deviance", "Residual deviance", "LR chi-square",
    "LR degrees of freedom", "LR p-value", "AIC", "McFadden pseudo-R²"
  ),
  Value = c(
    sum(weights(model, type = "prior")),
    round(model$null.deviance, 3), round(model$deviance, 3),
    round(model$null.deviance - model$deviance,          3),
    model$df.null -  model$df.residual, scales::pvalue(
      pchisq(model$null.deviance - model$deviance,
             df = model$df.null  - model$df.residual,    lower.tail = FALSE),
      accuracy  = 0.001
    ),                             round(AIC(model),     3),
    round(1 -     model$deviance / model$null.deviance,  3)
  )
)                                                                            %>%
knitr::kable(
  digits  = 3,
  caption = "Logistic regression goodness-of-fit and likelihood-ratio test"
)
```

## Discussion of Potential Bias

The findings in the report, despite the use of rigorous methodology, are subject
to several potential biases, the first group of which is data-related. On the
one hand, the original (raw) dataset comprises `r number_fmt(n_na)` missing
cells, to which the recoding of placeholders (e.g., "UNKNOWN", "(null)", and
"1022") added further `NA` values, namely, in the victim characteristics. Since
statistical models, including `glm()`, dropped rows with missing values by
default, the logistic regression was estimated on a smaller subset of victims
(29,624, see Table 4), which might have introduced selection bias if the missing
values were not randomly distributed, in addition to the loss of information for
estimation. On the other hand, aggregation to monthly frequency discarded
the within-month and hourly variability (`OCCUR_TIME`), while aggregation across
`BOROUGH` and `MONTH` for the classification model assumed constant odds
between `r m_min` and `r m_max`. Moreover, the data itself might also have been
a source of bias due to how it was collected and compiled into the original
dataset.

The second group of potential biases is method-related, given that the three
statistical hypotheses were tested with basic (textbook) procedures, and more
advanced models could be employed. First, the linear trends in Table 1 did not
account for potential unit roots, seasonality of `SHOOTINGS`, and violations of
Gauss-Markov assumptions, which might have produced biased or spurious estimates
-- e.g., a (seasonal) ARIMA could be a more adequate model. Second, given the
data limitations, the logistic regression included only four predictors (and
levels thereof) and its McFadden's pseudo-$R^2$ of 0.015 hinted at possible
omission of relevant predictors, potentially contributing to the bias. Hence,
although these limitations do not necessarily invalidate the findings, they
merit further statistical investigation (which is, however, beyond the scope of
this short report).

## Conclusion

This brief report examined `r number_fmt(sum(NYPD$SHOOTINGS))` shooting
incidents recorded by the NYPD, which took place between `r m_min` and
`r m_max` and out of which ca. `r round(murders * 100, 1)`% were classified as
murders, and answered the three research questions with the help of formal
statistical hypotheses tested at the 5% significance level ($\alpha=0.05$).
First, in terms of long-term trends (1), monthly time series exhibited a
declining linear trend for the City of New York as a whole and for four of the
five boroughs, with the steepest slope (i.e., decline) in Brooklyn, leading to
acceptance of **H1** in all cases except Manhattan (see Table 1) -- although the
low $R^2$ values and a citywide spike in incidents during the COVID-19 pandemic
(see Figure 1) merit further investigation. Second, in terms of the spatial
structure (2), shooting incidents were found to be concentrated in a small
number of precincts, namely, in the Bronx and Brooklyn (see Figure 2), and
Pearson's $\chi^2$ goodness-of-fit tests rejected the uniform distribution for
each borough and the dataset as a whole (see Table 2), i.e., leading to 
rejection of **H2**. Third, in terms of murder classification (3), the logistic
regression statistically supported **H3**: the odds of a murder incident
differed significantly across precincts (e.g., 28 precincts exhibited lower odds
when compared to Precinct 1) and increased with victim age (up to 169% higher
odds when compared to victims under 18), while victim sex and race were not
found to be statistically significant (see Table 3), a finding also confirmed
by an LR test (see Table 4). Still, McFadden's pseudo-$R^2$ of 0.015 suggested
limited explanatory power of geography and victim demographics. To sum up, in
light of the potential data-related and method-related biases, the findings of
the report should be interpreted with caution; hence, the use of more advanced
time-series models, as well as additional predictors, is recommended.
